note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Utilise sensory skills in beauty service for optimal client experience

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which five senses can a beauty worker use to improve the client's experience?
options: Sight, speech, touch, smell and memory
Hearing, balance, sight, smell and speech
Touch, taste, memory, sight and balance
Sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste

questions.stem: Why is good lighting important at the work station?
options: It makes the salon look bigger and more costly
It keeps the room warmer for the client
It saves electricity during the day
It lets you see the work clearly and spot problems

questions.stem: What can you learn by watching a client's body language during a service?
options: How much money she has with her
Whether she is comfortable, tense or in pain
What she will eat for dinner
Which of the other stylists she likes best in the salon

questions.stem: A client keeps blinking and rubbing her eyes while you use a hair spray. What does this suggest?
options: The spray is reaching her eyes and you should shield her face
She is very tired after a long day and simply wants to go to sleep
She likes the smell of the spray
She wants a different hairstyle

questions.stem: How should you use touch at the start of a service?
options: Touch the client suddenly from behind so that she stays alert
Avoid touching the client at all during the service
Tell her what you will do, then use a calm, firm touch
Use cold, wet hands to wake the client up

questions.stem: During a scalp massage, how do you know the pressure is right?
options: Use the same pressure on every client
Press as hard as you can for best results
Ask the client and watch her reaction
Wait until the client complains loudly about the pain

questions.stem: Why do you test the water temperature on your wrist before rinsing a client's hair?
options: To make sure it is comfortable and will not scald
To save as much hot water as possible for the next client
To clean your own hands
Because the client cannot feel water

questions.stem: What can you feel when you run your fingers through a client's hair?
options: How much money she paid for her last hair service
Whether she has had breakfast
The colour of her natural pigment
Whether the hair is dry, rough, oily or tangled

questions.stem: Before you touch a client for a massage, what should you do?
options: Start straight away so as not to waste any of her time
Explain what you will do and check she is happy
Ask another stylist to watch
Turn off all the lights

questions.stem: You smell burning hair while using a flat iron. What should you do at once?
options: Lift the iron away and check the heat setting and the hair
Spray perfume to cover the smell
Press harder to finish faster
Open the door and window, then carry on as before with the iron

questions.stem: A client says strong fragrances give her headaches. What should you do?
options: Use extra perfume around her chair to cover the chemical smells
Tell her she will get used to it
Choose fragrance-free products where possible and ventilate
Light a scented candle near her chair

questions.stem: Why should strong chemical smells in the salon be reduced?
options: They make the products work faster
Fumes can harm breathing and make clients feel unwell
They make the salon look dirty
They cost the salon a lot more money in its electricity bills

questions.stem: You smell gas near the salon's gas water heater. What should you do?
options: Light a match to find where the leak is
Switch on the fan heater to clear the air
Ignore it unless it gets stronger
No flames or switches, open windows, get everyone out and report it

questions.stem: Why do you check that towels and gowns smell fresh before use?
options: Because clients like a strong perfume on towels
So that you can reuse them many more times
Because smell shows the colour of the towel
A stale smell can mean they are not clean

questions.stem: What is active listening?
options: Talking while the client is speaking
Giving full attention and checking you understood
Listening to your favourite music loudly during the service
Hearing only the parts you agree with

questions.stem: How loud should background music be in the salon?
options: As loud as possible, to create energy in the whole salon
Off at all times, in silence
Low enough for clients and staff to talk easily
Loud enough to cover the sound of the dryers

questions.stem: A hood dryer starts making a loud rattling noise. What should you do?
options: Switch it off, take it out of use and report it
Turn the music up so the client cannot hear it
Hit it until the noise stops
Keep using it until the end of the day, then check it

questions.stem: How does your tone of voice affect the client?
options: It has no effect if your words are polite
A calm, warm tone helps her feel relaxed and welcome
A loud, fast voice shows the client that you are busy and skilled
A whisper makes the client trust you more

questions.stem: You offer a client a drink and a snack during a long service. What should you check first?
options: That she has paid in advance
That the snack you offer is the most expensive one in stock
That other clients cannot see
Whether she has any food allergies or needs

questions.stem: Why should drinks be kept away from the chemical products at the work station?
options: So that chemicals are not spilled into drinks or swallowed
Because drinks make the products work faster
So that the drinks stay cold
Because the smell of the chemicals spoils the taste of the tea

questions.stem: Which room temperature helps clients feel comfortable during a long service?
options: As cold as the air conditioning can possibly make the room
Hot, with all windows closed
Comfortably cool, with a light cover offered if needed
It does not matter in a hot country

questions.stem: What gives the best first impression when a client walks in?
options: Hair on the floor and used towels on chairs
A clean salon and a warm greeting
Staff eating lunch at the stations
Loud phone calls at the front desk

questions.stem: Why should clutter be cleared from the work station?
options: It looks untidy and can cause accidents
It makes the salon too quiet
It stops hair products from working
It makes the mirrors steam up

questions.stem: Mrs Morgan, who is blind, comes for a manicure. How can you help her?
options: Speak louder than usual
Guide her quickly by holding her shoulders and pushing her into the chair
Talk only to her companion
Introduce yourself, offer your arm and describe each step

questions.stem: How can you help a client who is deaf or hard of hearing?
options: Shout into her ear
Turn your back and talk normally
Face her, speak clearly and use notes or gestures
Avoid talking to her at all during the whole service

questions.stem: A client tells you that bright light and loud noise upset her. What should you do?
options: Tell her to wear earphones
Ask her to come back another day
Offer a quieter seat, softer light and calm explanations
Speed up the service as much as you can so she can leave sooner

questions.stem: During a long braiding session, what should you do to keep the client comfortable?
options: Keep going without a break to finish faster
Pull the braids tighter at the roots so that the style lasts longer
Ask her to hold her head still without moving
Offer short breaks, check her neck and ask about tension

questions.stem: A client says her new braids feel very tight and her scalp is sore. What should you do?
options: Loosen or redo the tight braids and check the scalp
Tell her they will loosen in a week
Give her a painkiller from your own bag and carry on
Spray oil on top and carry on

questions.stem: Which is a non-verbal sign that a client is happy with her service?
options: She keeps checking her watch and phone
She smiles and looks closely at the mirror
She crosses her arms and frowns
She avoids eye contact and sighs

questions.stem: Why do you ask the client for feedback at the end of the service?
options: To sell her a more costly service next time
To fill in time while she pays
Because the law says you must
To check she is happy and learn how to improve

questions.stem: A client says the water was too hot during the shampoo. What is the best reply?
options: That's how everyone likes it
You really should have told me that much earlier in the shampoo
Thank you for telling me; I will check it more carefully
The water heater is not my job

questions.stem: How can your sense of touch, through gloves, help keep a client safe during a chemical service?
options: By feeling the product to see if it is fresh
By noticing heat or swelling on the scalp and asking about stinging
By touching the chemical with bare hands to check it
By rubbing the scalp hard to spread the product

questions.stem: During a relaxer, the client says her scalp is burning. What should you do?
options: Rinse the product off at once with plenty of lukewarm water
Tell her to wait until the timer ends
Fan her scalp to cool it
Add more product to finish faster

questions.stem: Why must essential oils be used with care in a beauty service?
options: They are strong and can irritate skin or cause allergies
They have no effect on the skin at all
They always make clients fall asleep during the treatment
They can be swallowed safely

questions.stem: How should essential oils be used on the skin?
options: Neat, straight from the bottle
Diluted in a carrier oil, as the maker's instructions say
Mixed with a little nail polish remover so that they spread
Heated until they smoke

questions.stem: A comb at the station has hair and grease on it. What does this tell the client?
options: That the salon is very busy and popular
That the comb is new
That the salon may not be clean or safe
That the stylist is very skilled

questions.stem: Which is a suitable use of touch in a beauty service?
options: Hugging a new client without asking
Touching parts of the body that are not needed for the service
Patting the client's face to wake her
Touching only the areas needed, with the client's agreement

questions.stem: Why should you ask, not assume, how a client likes her natural hair handled and styled?
options: Because all clients really want exactly the same style in the end
So that the service takes longer
So that you can charge more
Because hair can have personal, cultural or religious meaning

questions.stem: How can you check that a finished hairstyle looks even?
options: Ask the next client what she thinks
Check it in the mirror from the front, sides and back
Look only at the front
Feel it all over with your eyes closed to check the balance

questions.stem: You notice the client looks pale and sweaty and says she feels faint. What should you do?
options: Stop, sit or lay her safely, give air and get first-aid help
Finish the service as quickly as you can so that she can go home
Give her a strong coffee and carry on
Turn up the hood dryer to warm her

questions.stem: Which choice of salon music suits most clients best?
options: Very loud music with rude lyrics to create a party mood
Whatever the stylist likes best that day
Calm music at a low volume, suited to the clients
News programmes turned up high

questions.stem: How should the client's head be supported at the shampoo basin?
options: Resting on the hard edge of the basin with no towel
Held up by the client's own neck muscles
On a towel or neck rest so the neck is comfortable
Pushed down firmly into the basin

questions.stem: What is the main aim of using sensory skills in a beauty service?
options: To give a safe, comfortable service the client enjoys
To make the service quicker
To sell more products
To impress the other staff and the salon manager with your skills

questions.stem: How should you greet a client who has just arrived?
options: Keep working and say nothing until you are free
Smile, say hello, use her name and offer a seat
Shout from across the salon
Ask her to wait outside until you are ready

questions.stem: Why should you note a client's preferences, such as music or massage pressure, on her record card?
options: So that you can share them with other salons in the area
To charge her for each preference
To remind her of her mistakes
So that the next visit can be made just as comfortable

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name for the messages we give with our face, hands and posture rather than with words?
Which of the five senses does a client use when she enjoys a cup of tea during her service?
What one word means a client's agreement to be touched or treated?
What word describes the overall feeling of a salon, created by its lighting, music, smells and decor?
Which massage movement is a light, slow stroking used to relax the client?
Which sense helps you feel that a client's shoulders are tense during a massage?
What sheet from the maker gives a product's hazards and first-aid steps?
What word means treating every client fairly, whatever their race, religion, age or disability?
What sign language is used by many deaf people in Jamaica?
What is the word for understanding and sharing how another person feels?
What kind of light is best for checking the true colour of hair or nail polish?
What word describes how hard or softly your hands press during a massage?
Which massage movement uses light, quick tapping with the fingertips?
What word means being on time for the client's appointment?
Which sense do you use to notice that a client's skin has gone red during a treatment?

essays.stem: Explain how a beauty worker can use each of the five senses to give a client a better experience. Give one example for each sense.
essays.modelAnswer: Sight: I look at the client's body language and face to see if she is relaxed, tense or in pain, and I check my work in good light from every side. A clean, tidy, well-lit salon also looks welcoming. Hearing: I listen carefully to what the client says and how she says it, and I keep music low so that we can talk. I also listen for warning sounds, such as a dryer rattling. Touch: I use a calm, confident touch, check the pressure in a massage and test water and tools on my wrist so they are comfortable. I feel the hair and skin to check their condition. Smell: I make sure towels and the salon smell fresh, offer fragrance-free products to sensitive clients, and notice warning smells such as burning hair or gas. Taste: I offer water or a drink during a long service, after checking for allergies, and keep drinks away from chemicals.
markingPoints: Sight: body language, checking work, clean well-lit salon
Hearing: listening to the client, music volume, warning sounds
Touch: calm touch, pressure, temperature checks, feeling hair and skin
Smell: fresh towels, fragrance-free options, warning smells
Taste: refreshments, allergy check, kept away from chemicals

essays.stem: Describe how you would create a pleasant, relaxing atmosphere in the salon for clients.
essays.modelAnswer: The atmosphere starts with cleanliness. Floors are swept after each client, stations are cleared and wiped, and used towels go straight into a covered bin. Lighting should be bright enough to work safely at the stations, with softer light in waiting and relaxing areas. Music should be calm, clean and low enough for people to talk, and the television, phones and staff voices should be kept down. The room should be comfortably cool, with fans or air conditioning set so that clients under hood dryers or wet from the basin do not get cold, and a light cover should be offered. Smells matter: the salon should be well ventilated so chemical fumes are carried away, towels should smell fresh, and strong scents should be avoided because some clients react to them. Comfortable chairs, neck rests at the basin, magazines, Wi-Fi and a glass of water help clients relax. Staff should greet every client warmly and look neat and professional.
markingPoints: Clean, tidy stations and floors; used towels removed
Suitable lighting for work and for relaxing
Calm music at a low volume; noise kept down
Comfortable temperature and fresh, ventilated air with mild or no scent
Comfortable seating, refreshments and a warm, professional welcome

essays.stem: Explain how to use touch professionally and safely in beauty services.
essays.modelAnswer: Touch is a large part of most beauty services, so it must always be professional. First I explain what I am going to do and check that the client agrees. I wash and dry my hands, keep my nails short and warm my hands if they are cold. I begin with a calm, confident touch, never a sudden one, and keep contact smooth during a massage. I ask about pressure and watch the client's face and body for signs of discomfort, then adjust. I test the temperature of water, wax, oils and hot tools on my own wrist before they touch the client. I touch only the areas needed for the service and keep the client covered and her privacy respected. I avoid areas with cuts, sores, swelling or infection. If the client asks me to stop or seems unhappy, I stop at once and ask what is wrong. Some clients, for cultural, religious or personal reasons, prefer less touch, and I respect this.
markingPoints: Explains first and gets the client's consent
Clean, warm hands, short nails, calm and smooth touch
Checks and adjusts pressure; watches for discomfort
Tests temperature of water, wax, oils and tools first
Touches only needed areas, avoids broken or infected skin, stops when asked, respects preferences

essays.stem: Explain how a beauty worker's senses can help to keep clients and staff safe. Give examples for at least four senses.
essays.modelAnswer: My senses warn me of danger before it becomes an accident. With sight I notice redness, swelling or a rash on the skin or scalp, which may mean a reaction, and I see spills on the floor, damaged cables or a client who looks pale and faint. With smell I notice burning hair from a tool that is too hot, strong chemical fumes that mean the room needs more air, or gas, in which case I avoid flames and switches, open windows, get everyone out and report it. With hearing I notice a dryer or steamer making a strange noise, which means it should be switched off and reported, and I hear a client say that something stings or burns. With touch, through gloves, I can feel heat on the scalp, and I test water, wax and tools on my wrist to avoid burns. If a client says a chemical is burning, I rinse it off at once. Staying alert with all my senses helps me act quickly and follow the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Sight: reactions, spills, damaged equipment, unwell client
Smell: burning hair, fumes, gas, with correct action
Hearing: faulty equipment and client complaints
Touch: heat on scalp, testing temperature on the wrist
Acts quickly and correctly, such as rinsing a burning chemical, and follows rules

essays.stem: Describe verbal and non-verbal communication with clients, and explain how to listen actively.
essays.modelAnswer: Verbal communication is what we say and how we say it. I use plain, polite words, a calm and warm tone, and a clear voice that is not too loud or too fast. I use the client's name and avoid trade words she may not understand. Non-verbal communication is the message we give without words: eye contact, facial expression, posture, gestures and how close we stand. I smile, face the client or meet her eyes in the mirror, nod to show I am listening, and keep an open posture. I also read the client's body language, such as crossed arms, frowning, or pulling away, which may show she is unhappy or in pain. Active listening means giving the client my full attention, not interrupting, and not thinking about my reply while she talks. I ask open questions, nod, and repeat back or sum up what she said to check that I have understood. Then I act on what I have heard.
markingPoints: Verbal: plain words, warm tone, clear voice, client's name
Non-verbal: eye contact, smile, posture, gestures
Reading the client's body language
Active listening: full attention, no interrupting
Open questions and repeating back to check understanding

essays.stem: Explain how you would adapt a service for a client who is blind or partly sighted, and for a client who is deaf or hard of hearing.
essays.modelAnswer: For a client who is blind or partly sighted, I introduce myself by name when she arrives and offer my arm to guide her, telling her about steps, corners and the chair. I never push or pull her. I explain each step before I do it, for example 'I am going to put a cape around your shoulders now', so that nothing comes as a surprise. I let her feel products or tools if she wants to, describe the result clearly at the end, and keep her bag and stick where she can reach them. I keep walkways clear. For a client who is deaf or hard of hearing, I face her when I speak, in good light, so that she can see my lips and face, and I speak clearly but do not shout. I turn down the music and dryers while we talk. I use gestures, write notes or use my phone, and learn a few basic signs of Jamaican Sign Language if I can. I check that she has understood and agree simple signals for 'stop' or 'too hot'.
markingPoints: Blind client: introduces self, offers arm, never pushes, clear walkways
Explains each step before touching
Describes the result and keeps belongings within reach
Deaf client: faces her in good light, speaks clearly, reduces noise
Uses notes, gestures or sign language and agrees signals; checks understanding

essays.stem: Explain how to use fragrances and essential oils safely in beauty services.
essays.modelAnswer: Fragrances and essential oils can make a service feel special, but they are strong chemicals and some clients react to them. At the consultation I ask about allergies, asthma, headaches from scents, skin problems, pregnancy and medical conditions, and I write the answers on the record card. I offer fragrance-free products to anyone who prefers them. Essential oils must never be used neat on the skin. They are diluted in a carrier oil as the maker's instructions say, and some oils should not be used for certain clients, such as during pregnancy, so I check the maker's guidance. Where the maker says, I do a skin test first. I avoid the eyes and broken skin. I use only a small amount, keep the room ventilated, and do not burn oils near clients who are sensitive. If the skin becomes red or itchy, I stop and remove the product. Oils are stored closed, labelled, cool and out of reach of children.
markingPoints: Asks about allergies, asthma, pregnancy and conditions, and records them
Offers fragrance-free options
Essential oils diluted in a carrier oil as the maker says; checks who should not use them
Skin test where the maker says; avoids eyes and broken skin; ventilation
Stops if a reaction happens; stores oils safely

essays.stem: A client looks unhappy and says the service is not what she wanted. Describe how you would handle this.
essays.modelAnswer: I notice her body language, such as frowning or looking away, and stop what I am doing. I speak calmly and kindly, and if possible move to a quieter spot so that she does not feel embarrassed. I ask open questions, such as 'Can you tell me what you were hoping for?', and listen actively without interrupting or arguing. I show empathy, for example 'I can see why you are disappointed', and thank her for telling me. I repeat back what she wants so that we agree on the problem. Then I offer a fair solution within my role, such as adjusting the style, redoing a nail or changing the products, and I check the time with her. If I cannot fix it, or she asks for a refund, I call the supervisor and follow the salon's complaints procedure. I note what happened and what was agreed on her record card, and I learn from the feedback to improve my consultations.
markingPoints: Notices body language and stops; speaks calmly, in private
Asks open questions and listens without arguing
Shows empathy, thanks her and repeats back to agree the problem
Offers a fair solution, or refers to the supervisor and complaints procedure
Records the outcome and learns from the feedback

essays.stem: Describe the client's journey from arriving at the salon to leaving, and how sensory skills make each stage a good experience.
essays.modelAnswer: When the client arrives, she should see a clean, tidy salon and be greeted with a smile and her name within a short time. The waiting area should be comfortable, with calm music and fresh air, and she should be offered water and told how long she will wait. At the consultation, I sit with her in good light, use open questions, listen actively and look at and feel her hair, skin or nails. During the service I explain each step, use a calm touch, check pressure and temperature, and watch her body language for discomfort. I keep music and dryers at a comfortable level and offer breaks or a drink during long services. At the end, I show her the result in the mirror from all sides, ask for her feedback, and give aftercare advice in plain words. At the desk, payment is quick and friendly, and I offer to book her next visit. I note her preferences on the record card so the next visit feels just as good.
markingPoints: Arrival: clean salon, warm greeting by name, comfortable waiting area
Consultation: good light, open questions, active listening
Service: explains steps, calm touch, checks comfort, manages noise, offers breaks
Finish: shows result, asks for feedback, aftercare advice
Departure and records: friendly payment, rebooking, preferences noted

essays.stem: Explain how you keep a client comfortable during a long service, such as braiding or a chemical service.
essays.modelAnswer: Before I start, I tell the client how long the service will take, suggest she uses the washroom, and make sure she is seated comfortably with her back and feet supported and the chair at the right height. I check the room temperature and offer a light cover if the air conditioning is cool. During the service I check in often, asking 'Are you comfortable?' and watching for signs of tension, such as a stiff neck, fidgeting or wincing. In braiding, I avoid pulling too tightly at the roots and edges, and I loosen any braid that feels sore. In a chemical service, I ask regularly about stinging or burning and act at once if she feels it. I offer short breaks to stretch, and water or a snack after checking for allergies, kept away from the chemicals. I keep music low and let her rest quietly if she prefers. I tell her how far we have got so she knows what to expect.
markingPoints: Explains the time and seats the client comfortably with support
Manages temperature and offers a cover
Checks in often and watches for tension or pain
Avoids tight braiding; acts at once on stinging in chemical services
Offers breaks and refreshments safely, and keeps her informed

practical1.title: Set up a sensory-friendly station and give a relaxing hand or scalp massage
practical1.brief: As a group, plan and set up one salon station and a small waiting corner that appeal to all five senses. Write a short sensory plan sheet together: lighting, music and volume, fresh towels and air, fragrance-free options, a drink offered after an allergy check, and how you will check the client's comfort. Each member is responsible for one sense and sets up that part. Then work in pairs, on members who agree: each member greets their partner by name, explains what they will do, gets consent, checks for contraindications, and gives a short relaxing hand massage or scalp massage, asking about pressure and watching body language. Each 'client' fills in a short feedback form. Swap so every member gives and receives. Photos show hands, hair, the station and the forms only, never faces.
materials: Salon station, chair and a small waiting area
Fresh towels, a light cover and a neck rest
Lamp or adjustable lighting, and a speaker for low music
Fragrance-free hand cream or massage cream, and a scalp oil
Sensory plan sheet, client feedback forms and pens
photos: The completed group sensory plan sheet
The station and waiting corner set up, showing lighting and fresh towels
The refreshments and fragrance-free products set out
A member greeting and explaining the service (hands and setting only)
The hand or scalp massage in progress
The station cleaned and tidied afterwards
checklist: Set up their sense area as planned and explained how it helps the client
Greeted the client by name and explained the service before touching
Asked for consent and checked for contraindications
Used clean, warm hands and a calm, smooth touch
Asked about pressure and adjusted it, watching body language
Kept music and voice at a comfortable level
Offered a drink after checking for allergies, away from products
Asked for feedback and recorded the client's preferences
safety: Check for cuts, sores or infection before massage, and do not massage over them
Use fragrance-free products for anyone who reacts to scents; ask about nut and other allergies
Keep cables, drinks and water spills away from walkways and electrical items
Clean and disinfect the station and tools after each partner

practical2.title: Client journey role plays for clients with different sensory needs
practical2.brief: As a group, act out the full client journey (arrival, consultation, service, checking the result, feedback and departure) for four clients with different needs. Use these role-play clients: (1) Mrs Morgan, who is blind; (2) Kevin, who is deaf and uses Jamaican Sign Language and notes; (3) Miss Henry, who gets headaches from strong scents and loud noise; (4) a nervous first-time client who has had a bad salon experience. Each member plays the beauty worker once, while others play the client and observer. Before each role play, the worker writes a short plan of how they will adapt the journey using all five senses. The observer fills in a note sheet. For the service part, act it out with a comb or a hand massage, with no chemicals. Photograph each stage with the notes, and hand in the plans, note sheets and photos.
materials: Salon chair, mirror, cape, towels and a comb
Paper, pens, and a phone for typed notes
Adaptation plan sheets and observer note sheets
photos: The arrival and greeting stage of a role play
The consultation stage, for example with written notes for the deaf client
The service stage, showing guiding, explaining or a quiet set-up
The result being shown and feedback being asked for
checklist: Wrote a clear plan that adapts the journey to the client's needs
Greeted the client suitably, for example introducing themselves to a blind client
Communicated in a way the client could follow (face to face, notes, gestures, plain words)
Explained each step before touching and checked consent
Adjusted light, sound and smell to suit the client
Checked comfort and body language throughout
Asked for feedback and responded with empathy
As observer, wrote fair, useful notes
safety: No chemicals, hot tools or sharp tools are used in the role plays
When guiding a 'blind' client, walk slowly, offer your arm and keep walkways clear
Keep the role-play area tidy so nobody trips
Treat each other with respect and do not make fun of any disability
